newsitem.title: USA: ABMS copper data revisions may spur forecast rejig.
newsitem.headline: ABMS copper data revisions may spur forecast rejig.

text.p: The American Bureau of Metal Statistics' decision to sharply revise its copper producer stock data will prompt some forecasters to rejig their numbers and be bullish for prices, analyst Fred Demler of E D and F Man International said.

The ABMS has just unveiled its revised copper data, showing that as of October 1996, refinery copper stocks outside the U.S. stood at 161,700 short tons compared to a previous total of 842,600 short tons, a downward revision of 680,900 short tons.
"It has significant implications for the copper market. It's very bullish," Demler said.
"I have confidence in the new figures and confidence in saying that inventories are at extremely low levels relative to where they have been in the last 25 years," Demler added.

Adding the new ABMS figure to COMEX, LME and merchant inventories, the stock/consumption ratio tumbles to 2.7 weeks of usage which should translate into a copper price of 130 to 140 cents per pound, Demler said.
"Historically the stock/consumption ratio has never dipped below 3 weeks," Demler said.
The ABMS have only revised their producer inventory from 1994, Demler said. "I think the data went bad in 1987," he added.
ABMS executive director Brian Simpson said the way data was gathered has been changed after errors were found, but the alterations to data collection may not be complete.
"It's a work in progress," Simpson said. "But we have more reporting companies now than we ever did in the past, but it's still not complete. There is still work to do."
The ABMS relied too much on estimates from third parties rather that getting data direct from producers. Data on China was still problematic, Simpson said.
Data on the U.S. copper industry was no problem, Simpson added.

Nevertheless, in a previous report dated December 3, 1996 the ABMS showed U.S. refinery stocks in October 1996 totaling 40,700 short tons, but this falls to a revised 13,000 short tons in the newly-released report.
Analysts have been complaining about copper data for some time. Lisbon-based International Copper Study Group has been taking steps to improve the quality of its copper data.

U.K-based World Bureau of Metal Statistics prompted an outcry late last year when it suggested there may be a huge hidden hoard of copper in Rotterdam warehouses. Dutch customs officials later admitted errors in their red metal paper trails.

Simpson said a draft of the revised figures was sent to several analysts for comment. "The comments that came back were very positive...People felt there was a problem in the past and some type of change needed to be made."

Demler said previous talk that possible market manipulation lay behind high prices in the past may now be mistaken. With inventories much lower than people thought, fundamentals were better than they appeared.
